title: Grade 8 Integrated Science Scheme of Work: Ecosystems and Interdependence (Synthetic Mock Corpus)
subject: Integrated Science

entries.topic: Ecosystems and interdependence: Habitats, populations and communities
priorKnowledge: Plants and animals live in different places
learningOutcomes: Define habitat, population, community and ecosystem
Classify environmental factors as biotic or abiotic
Use a quadrat to estimate the number of plants in two different areas
keyConcepts: habitat is the place where an organism lives
population is all organisms of one species in an area
community is all populations living in an area
ecosystem is a community together with its non-living environment
biotic factors are living (predators, food, competition)
abiotic factors are non-living (light, temperature, water, soil)
learningActivities: Learners sample plants in a sunny and a shaded area of the school grounds using randomly placed quadrats
Learners calculate the mean number of plants per quadrat for each area
Learners list biotic and abiotic factors that might explain differences
Learners sort example factors into biotic and abiotic
entries.assessment: Define habitat and give one biotic factor and one abiotic factor affecting organisms in a pond.
entries.teacherNotes: Learners confuse habitat with ecosystem. Make clear a habitat is where a species lives, while an ecosystem includes all organisms and the non-living environment. Learners often think abiotic factors are not important to living things. Stress random placement of quadrats to avoid bias.

entries.topic: Ecosystems and interdependence: Food chains and food webs
priorKnowledge: Plants make their own food using sunlight
Animals feed on plants or other animals
learningOutcomes: Construct food chains with arrows pointing in the direction of energy transfer
Identify producers, primary consumers, secondary consumers and decomposers
Predict the effects of removing one organism from a food web
keyConcepts: arrows show the direction of energy transfer from the organism eaten to the organism that eats it
food web is a set of linked food chains
learningActivities: Learners create a food web with yarn using organism cards (grass, grasshopper, zebra, frog, snake, lion, fungi)
Learners identify each organism's trophic role
Learners remove one organism and predict effects on others
Learners draw a food chain from their own local ecosystem
entries.assessment: In the food chain grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, identify the producer and the secondary consumer and predict what happens to grasshoppers if all frogs die.
entries.teacherNotes: Learners often draw arrows in the wrong direction, pointing from the eater to the food. Learners may think the Sun is a producer; producers are organisms that make food by photosynthesis. Learners may assume removing a predator only benefits the prey; indirect effects on other organisms should be discussed.

entries.topic: Ecosystems and interdependence: Interdependence and human impact
learningOutcomes: Explain interdependence using pollination and predator-prey relationships
Describe how deforestation, pollution and overfishing affect ecosystems
Suggest actions that can protect ecosystems
learningActivities: Learners run a predator-prey simulation with beans or cards and graph both populations
Learners analyse a case study of pesticide use that reduces insect pollinators
Learners trace the impact of one human activity through a food web
Learners propose a conservation action plan for a local ecosystem
entries.assessment: Explain how the loss of bees from a meadow could affect both plants and animals.
entries.teacherNotes: Learners often believe losing one species does not affect others. Learners also think predator and prey populations change independently. Use graphs to show linked cycles. Choose case studies relevant to learners' own region where possible.
